When to say no to a project

Four signals that a project will cost more than it pays, and how to decline well.

Jonas Weber · 13 Aug 2026

Illustration · Web Academy studio

Most courses are built as a library: a hundred videos and a search box. It looks generous and it is quietly hostile, because the learner has to design the sequence themselves.

A cohort does the opposite. It fixes the order, the pace and the room, then asks you to show your work in front of people who will tell you the truth about it.

What a cohort buys you

Three things you cannot get from a video: a deadline, an audience, and a person who notices when you stop.

Learning is a social act with a technical component, not the other way around.

The structure is simple. Six weeks. One live session a week. One piece of work every fortnight, reviewed against a written rubric that you receive at the start.

Where this goes wrong

Cohorts fail when they are treated as group video calls: no agenda, no artefact, no standard. The fix is boring — publish the rubric, keep the room small, and make the first session produce something.

That is the whole idea. The rest is scheduling.
